opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, because there's often a gap between what looks impressive on a benchmark and what actually moves the needle on the work I care about.

The way I tend to assess it is pretty empirical and personal: I just try to hand the AI real chunks of my actual work and see how far it gets before I have to step in. A lot of my work is research-y. It's reading a bunch of papers, synthesizing arguments, building rough quantitative models, writing up a case for some view about how AI development will go. So the question I ask isn't "can it solve this hard math problem" or "can it write this function." It's "if I gave this to a smart research assistant, how much of the task could they take off my plate, and how much would I have to redo?"

What I've noticed is that specialized capabilities, like being really good at coding or at a certain kind of reasoning puzzle, are useful but often aren't the bottleneck. The bottleneck is more like judgment and taste. Does it know which of the ten threads it could pull on actually matters? Does it notice when an assumption is doing a lot of work? Can it tell when its own output is subtly wrong? Those are much harder to measure, and models have historically been weaker there relative to how they look on narrow tests.

So I try to look at it in terms of time horizons and autonomy. Can it do a fifteen-minute task reliably? An hour-long task? A day-long task, where it has to make a bunch of intermediate decisions without checking in? That framing has been more predictive for me of real usefulness than any single capability score. A model can be superhuman at some narrow skill and still not save me much time if I have to babysit every step.

And the other thing I watch for is error profile. For a lot of the work I want help with, an assistant that's right ninety percent of the time but confidently wrong the other ten, in ways that are hard for me to spot, can actually be net negative, because the verification cost eats the gains. So I care a lot about whether the model's mistakes are legible.

Honestly, I think the field as a whole underinvests in this kind of measurement: careful, realistic evaluations of whether AI can do the actual messy, open-ended tasks people do at work, as opposed to clean, self-contained problems. That's partly why I've been interested in pushing for better evals of real-world task completion. Because the answer to "how useful is this for my work" ends up being pretty decision-relevant, both for me personally and for figuring out how close we are to AI meaningfully accelerating research, including AI research itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I try to be pretty empirical about it rather than reasoning from first principles about what the models "should" be able to do. The thing I've found is that benchmark performance and the kind of headline capabilities people talk about are surprisingly weakly correlated with how useful a model actually is for the specific work I'm trying to get done.

So the way I tend to approach it is, I have a set of tasks that are genuinely part of my job, things like doing a literature review on some question in AI forecasting, or drafting a section of a report, or critiquing an argument I'm making and finding the holes in it. And I just try the models on those tasks and see where they fall down. And what I've noticed is that the failure modes are often not the ones you'd predict from the benchmarks. A model can be superhuman at competition math and still kind of miss the point of what I'm asking in a fairly mundane way, or confidently assert something about a paper that it's clearly pattern-matching rather than actually having engaged with.

I think the deeper issue is that a lot of the work I care about has this property where the hard part is figuring out what the right question even is, or noticing that two things that look similar are actually importantly different. And that's a kind of judgment that's hard to measure in a benchmark because the benchmark itself has already done the work of specifying the problem cleanly. So I've become somewhat skeptical of "the model got X percent on this eval, therefore it can do my job." I think the right move is to actually sit with the model on real work and build up an intuition for where it's trustworthy and where it isn't.

And I'd say that intuition has shifted a lot over the past couple of years. There are things I now hand off without much thought that I would have checked carefully before. But there's also a pretty stubborn core of tasks, especially ones involving taste about what matters, where I still find the models more useful as a sparring partner than as something I can delegate to. I think that's actually a pretty important thing to track, because the question of when that core shrinks is in some sense the question I care most about for forecasting purposes.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how those capabilities fit into the work you actually want to get done. A system can be extremely good at a particular task, but if that task isn’t the bottleneck—or if it takes a lot of effort to specify the task and check the result—that might not translate into much practical value.

For the kinds of research I’d want help with, a lot of the difficulty is figuring out what question to ask, which evidence would change my mind, and whether an argument actually holds together. Specialized capabilities can help with pieces of that. But there’s a difference between being able to produce a useful piece of analysis when prompted carefully and being able to take a fairly ambiguous research question and make progress on it independently.

So I’d assess usefulness by looking at the whole workflow: How much can I delegate? How much supervision does it need? And how much better or faster is the final result once you account for the work of checking it?

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much those capabilities help with the actual work, rather than how impressive they are in isolation. A system might be very good at solving a well-specified problem, but a lot of what I want help with is figuring out which problem to work on, what assumptions matter, and whether an answer should change my mind.

So specialized capabilities can be really useful, especially when I can give the system a clear task and check its work. But if I have to spend a lot of time supplying context, breaking everything into little pieces, and catching subtle mistakes, that limits how much I can delegate. What I’d really value is a system that can handle more of that whole process reliably.
